argument: Nietzsche writes Thus Spoke Zarathustra as the natural continuation of the historical Zarathustra's thought, imagining that with better information the inventor of good-versus-evil would eventually conclude these categories are human inventions, not cosmic facts. The book's central teaching is that human development moves through three stages: the camel, who unquestioningly carries the weights of inherited tradition; the lion, who slays the dragon 'Thou Shalt' by saying no to those traditions but is left with nothing after clearing away the meaning they provided; and the child, who moves past that nihilistic stalemate by saying yes and creating new values and goals of its own. The overman is the ideal this process points toward, not a fixed endpoint but a permanent invitation to keep growing, the way present-day humans represent a further stage beyond our evolutionary ancestors.
keyIdeas: Nietzsche chose the historical Zarathustra, inventor of the good-versus-evil dichotomy, as his narrator because he imagines Zarathustra, given more information, would conclude that good and evil are human inventions rather than cosmic truths.

A 'weight' on the camel's back isn't defined by whether an action came from someone else's advice, but by whether you're doing it only because you were told to, without ever examining your own reasons.

The lion stage means slaying the dragon 'Thou Shalt' by questioning inherited traditions, but this also strips away the true-world theories that once gave life meaning, leaving many people stuck in nihilism.

The 'bad restaurant' mistake is concluding that because one particular meaning turned out to be false, there must be no meaning anywhere, rather than realizing you were simply looking in the wrong place.

The child stage is capable of saying yes and creating new values, unlike the lion which only knows how to say no; and the overman itself is never a final destination, only a continual invitation to keep growing.

terms.def: The ideal of continual self-overcoming Nietzsche says life is a constant pursuit toward, comparable to how present-day humans surpass their evolutionary ancestors.
The first stage of development: a person who unquestioningly carries the burdens and traditions others have placed on them.
The second stage: someone who recognizes inherited traditions as arbitrary and gains the courage to say no to them by slaying the dragon Thou Shalt.
The fire-breathing dragon representing all the inherited 'shoulds' and traditions the lion must slay to become self-aware.
The third stage: a person freed of imposed weights, capable of saying yes and creating new values and goals of their own, resembling a child at play.
Nietzsche's figure who avoids all discomfort and risk and calls himself happy, but whose happiness is shallow compared to happiness earned through struggle.

anchors: if only Zarathustra had been born into the time of Nietzsche when better information was available, the natural conclusion that he would have arrived at eventually is that these concepts of good and evil are nothing more than an invention by human beings
